metadata.note: Three historical, now-discontinued anthracite-region railroads that made Scranton, PA one of the busiest rail hubs in the Northeast, researched from Wikipedia and railroad-history sites in response to a question about historical service to Scranton. All predate any GTFS/live-data era and have no modern segment (no through passenger train serves Scranton today). Route geometry follows the real intermediate towns each railroad's own history describes, and is a simplified handful of waypoints rather than surveyed track centerline for the CNJ feature -- but the DL&W Hoboken-Scranton-Buffalo feature was RE-TRACED from OpenStreetMap on 2026-08-24 and is now mostly real track (see its geometry_quality property), and EXCEPT the Delaware and Hudson's Albany-Montreal feature, whose geometry was replaced with the full amtrak.geojson 'Adirondack' shape (Albany-Montreal portion only): that modern route runs on the same D&H right-of-way used historically by the Laurentian/Montreal Limited, per that feature's own segment notes, so it is a faithful stand-in rather than a straight-line approximation; and except the DL&W's Binghamton-Buffalo leg, densified to 17 waypoints (Owego, Waverly, Elmira, Corning, Painted Post, Savona, Bath, Cohocton, Wayland, Dansville, Mount Morris, Warsaw/Linwood, East Bethany, Alden, Depew) per the New York, Lackawanna and Western Railroad's 1882 station list, which closely paralleled the Erie Railroad's own line through the same towns. Era boundaries follow real corporate-history milestones (line openings, mergers, bankruptcy/discontinuation dates); headway_min and avg_speed_kmh within each era are estimates, not sourced from real timetables.
metadata.source: Wikipedia, american-rails.com, trains.com, bridge-line.org (see conversation for citations)

geometry_quality_by_feature.dlw-hoboken-scranton-buffalo: RE-TRACED 2026-08-24. 320.5 mi real OSM track + 81.6 mi of straight-line legs where the alignment is gone; total 404.0 mi against a documented ~395 mi (the old 25-point sketch drew 346.9 mi). Routed leg by leg through the DL&W's own station list: Hoboken, Newark Broad St, Summit, Morristown, Denville, Dover, Port Morris, Blairstown, Slateford Jct, Delaware Water Gap, Stroudsburg, Tobyhanna, Scranton, Clarks Summit, Nicholson, Hallstead, Binghamton, Owego, Waverly, Elmira, Corning, Painted Post, Bath, Wayland, Dansville, Mount Morris, Warsaw, Alden, Depew, Buffalo -- every one matched to within 1.1 km of the traced line. Abandoned/disused/razed OSM railway was allowed but mildly penalised so surviving track wins where both exist. Simplified with Douglas-Peucker at 20 m. Split 2026-08-24 into four era features (dlw-scranton-great-bend, dlw-southern-division, dlw-hoboken-binghamton, dlw-hoboken-scranton-buffalo), all slices of this same trace; cut indices 191 (Delaware Water Gap), 407 (Scranton), 568 (Great Bend), 599 (Binghamton).
geometry_quality_by_feature.cnj-jersey-city-scranton: NOT RE-TRACED. Still a 9-point waypoint sketch, not surveyed track centerline -- straight chords between towns. Treat its length and shape as indicative only.
geometry_quality_by_feature.dh-albany-montreal-laurentian: Borrowed geometry: the full amtrak.geojson 'Adirondack' shape (Albany-Montreal portion), which runs on the same D&H right-of-way used historically. A faithful stand-in rather than an approximation.

metadata.known_issues: RESOLVED 2026-08-24: the DL&W is now split into four construction-era features -- Scranton-Great Bend (1851-1856), the Southern Division to the Delaware Water Gap (1856-1868), Hoboken-Binghamton (1868-1882), and the full Hoboken-Buffalo main line (1882-1970) -- so the map no longer draws Buffalo, or a Hoboken terminal, before the DL&W actually had them. Dates verified: first segment Scranton-Great Bend opened December 20 1851; DL&W incorporated March 11 1853; Southern Division opened May 27 1856; Morris and Essex leased December 10 1868 (the M&E's own Hoboken alignment had entered regular service October 14 1863); New York, Lackawanna and Western opened Binghamton-Buffalo September 17 1882; main line 395 miles. REMAINING ISSUE: all four features draw the New Jersey portion on the 1911 Lackawanna Cut-Off corridor rather than the pre-1911 'Old Road' via Washington, so the 1868-1911 eras are on an alignment that did not yet exist; the Old Road has not been traced. All headway_min and avg_speed_kmh values in this file remain estimates, not timetable figures.
metadata.rule4_split_2026_08_24: Rule 4 ownership split. The Erie Railroad and the Delaware, Lackawanna & Western did not become one another -- they merged on October 17 1960 into a new company, the Erie Lackawanna Railroad (reorganized as the Erie Lackawanna Railway in 1968 under the Dereco holding company, and folded into Conrail April 1 1976). Before this pass the post-1960 years were still drawn in the predecessors' own colours, so one company appeared on the map in two different colours -- ex-Erie segments in Erie black #22223B, ex-Lackawanna in DL&W brown #7F5539. Every feature whose segments ran past 1960 has been split at the merger date into a second feature with identical geometry, company 'Erie Lackawanna Railroad', colour #A02C5A. Six features across six files: erie-mainline-jerseycity-buffalo, dlw-hoboken-scranton-buffalo, erie-salamanca-jamestown-dayton, erie-chicago-extension, erie-buffalo-niagara-falls, cmv-cleveland-youngstown. The NYS&W (nysw-jerseycity-stroudsburg) is deliberately NOT included -- it had reverted to independent operation by 1940 and was not part of the merger.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

properties.line: Delaware, Lackawanna & Western: Scranton – Great Bend (first segment)
properties.speed_source: estimated for 1850s steam on a new anthracite road; unsourced
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap; this stretch (Scranton-Clarks Summit-Nicholson-Hallstead/Great Bend) matched to surviving track with no straight-line legs.

segments.note: The first piece of what became the DL&W: opened December 20 1851 running north from Scranton to Great Bend, built to move Lackawanna Valley anthracite to the Erie Railroad at Great Bend. The Delaware, Lackawanna and Western itself was incorporated March 11 1853 by consolidating the Lackawanna and Western with the Delaware and Cobb's Gap. At this date there was no line east toward New Jersey at all. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.line: Delaware, Lackawanna & Western: Delaware Water Gap – Great Bend (Southern Division)
properties.speed_source: estimated for 1850s-60s steam over the Pocono grade; unsourced
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap end to end; no straight-line legs in this extent. NOTE the eastern end stops at the Delaware Water Gap because that is where DL&W's own rails ended in this era -- the onward connection across New Jersey via the Warren Railroad to the Central Railroad of New Jersey at Hampton Junction is NOT drawn.

segments.note: The Southern Division opened May 27 1856, carrying the line southeast from Scranton over the Poconos to the Delaware River. It gave Scranton a through route toward New York, but NOT over DL&W metals: beyond the Delaware, trains ran via the Warren Railroad and then the Central Railroad of New Jersey. The DL&W had no terminal of its own on the Hudson yet. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.speed_source: estimated for late-19th-century steam over this profile; unsourced
properties.geometry_quality: Mixed. East of the Delaware the route is largely real-traced OSM track (the surviving Morris & Essex / NJ Transit Morristown Line), but with straight-line approximations at Denville-Dover (3.8 mi) and Port Morris-Blairstown (10.6 mi); west of the Delaware the trace to Scranton and Binghamton is real track apart from Binghamton-Owego, which lies outside this feature's extent. GEOMETRY CAVEAT: the New Jersey portion drawn here follows the corridor of the 1911 Lackawanna Cut-Off (Port Morris-Slateford), NOT the pre-1911 'Old Road' via Washington that trains actually used in this era, and the Port Morris-Blairstown stretch of it is a straight-line approximation because the Cut-Off was lifted in 1979-80.

segments.note: On December 10 1868 the DL&W leased the Morris and Essex Railroad, finally giving it its own rails across northern New Jersey to a Hudson River terminal at Hoboken -- a terminal the M&E had opened to regular service on October 14 1863. From here the DL&W ran Hoboken to Binghamton on its own line. It still did not reach Buffalo. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

segments.note: Erie Lackawanna from the merger of October 17 1960; reorganized as the Erie Lackawanna Railway in 1968. EL consolidated its passenger operation on this ex-Lackawanna route and on Hoboken Terminal, and for a time ran the combined through train over it between Hoboken and Binghamton. The Phoebe Snow name was dropped October 28 1962, revived, and discontinued for good November 27 1966; all remaining passenger service on the former Lackawanna route via Scranton ended January 6 1970. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

segments.note: D&H extended its own line north from Albany to Rouses Point in 1876, connecting there with the Champlain & St. Lawrence Railroad for onward access to Montreal. (Note: an earlier version of this feature also plotted a Scranton-Nineveh Junction-Albany leg here, but that duplicated the more detailed Albany-Binghamton [Susquehanna Division] line and rested on a mistaken claim that Binghamton was a bypassed spur off Nineveh Junction; sources instead describe Albany-Binghamton as the real through route, with the Scranton/Penn Division branching off it at Nineveh. Trimmed to Albany-Montreal only, which is not otherwise represented.) estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The Laurentian (daytime) and Montreal Limited (overnight) became D&H's flagship trains from 1923, running New York-Albany-Montreal (the New York-Albany leg ran over connecting New York Central trackage). Both were discontinued Apr 30 1971 at Amtrak's creation; the D&H main line saw no passenger service for three years until Amtrak's Adirondack began Aug 6 1974. Still ran the same 1870 Ararat Summit/Lanesboro/Nineveh Junction routing south of Binghamton throughout this era. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
